The disciples' question -- 'who then is this, that wind and sea obey him?' -- has a scriptural answer they don't yet draw. The sleeping-figure-in-the-storm also recalls Jonah 1. CONFIDENCE: established for the Psalms; the deeper Baal/chaoskampf layer is probable and offered as available background, not asserted dependence.
scholarship: on chaoskampf: Day, God's Conflict with the Dragon and the Sea

references.speaker: other
references.source: 'Legion' as Roman military term; possible anti-imperial satire (the herd drowned in the sea; cf. Pharaoh's army, Exod 14-15)
references.note: The demons name themselves 'Legion, for we are many' -- legiOn is the Latin military unit (c. 6000 men). Many read a political resonance: the unclean occupying force, sent into unclean swine, charges into the SEA and drowns, as Pharaoh's army drowned in the Exodus (Exod 14-15). The pigs further evoke the boar emblem of Legio X Fretensis, stationed in the region. Offered as probable thematic resonance, not allegory-with-a-key; the exorcism's surface logic (naming the spirit, cf. III.1-a) stands regardless.
scholarship: Theissen, The Miracle Stories of the Early Christian Tradition
Myers, Binding the Strong Man (the political reading)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: tombs and the unclean as demon-haunt (cf. Isa 65:4); the sea/abyss as demonic destination (Luke 8:31, 'the abyss')
references.note: The demoniac among the tombs trades on the conception of graveyards and unclean places as demonic territory (cf. Isa 65:4, those who sit among graves). Luke makes the cosmology explicit: the demons beg not to be sent to 'the abyss' (8:31), the watery deep of confinement -- so their plunge into the sea returns them to the chaos-deep. Probable Second Temple demonology.
scholarship: on the abyss: Luke 8:31 with Fitzmyer AYB

VII.3.canon_title: Jairus's daughter and the hemorrhaging woman

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: menstrual/discharge impurity (Leviticus 15:25-30); the reversal of contagion
references.note: The woman with the twelve-year flow of blood is in a permanent state of ritual impurity (the zavah of Lev 15:25-30), which she transmits by touch -- so reaching for Jesus in a crowd is a transgressive act. The story inverts the expected flow of contagion: instead of her impurity defiling him, his power heals her. Historical-cultural background essential to the scene's tension. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Elijah/Elisha child-raisings (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:18-37); 'talitha koum' (Aramaic)
references.note: The raising of Jairus's daughter joins the Elijah/Elisha raising-pattern (1 Kgs 17; 2 Kgs 4, where Elisha raises a child behind closed doors and the parents are present) already exploited at Nain (V.2-a). 'The child is not dead but sleeping' and the Aramaic command 'talitha koum' ('little girl, arise') preserve the underlying word; the twelvefold motif (the woman's twelve years, the girl's twelve years) binds the intercalated stories. Probable.

VII.4.placement_flag: Duplicate-placement question with Luke 4:16-30 (II.9); see that entry. The 'prophet without honor' saying cross-refs II.7-b, II.9-c.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the prophet-without-honor logion (cross-ref II.7-b, II.9-c): Thomas 31 // P.Oxy 1.30-35
references.note: Mark's form -- 'a prophet is not without honor except in his own country and among his own kin and house' -- is the same multiply-attested logion handled at II.7-b (John 4:44) and II.9-c (Luke), independently present at Thomas 31 / P.Oxy 1. The rest of the pericope (the carpenter, son of Mary, the named siblings) is biographical, not allusive. Established by multiple attestation.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 31

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: inner-canon: Paul citing a dominical command (1 Cor 9:14; cf. 1 Tim 5:18); 'the laborer deserves his wages'
references.note: 'The laborer deserves his food/wages' (Matt 10:10 // Luke 10:7) is expressly cited by Paul as the Lord's own command: 'the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel' (1 Cor 9:14, mid-50s -- pre-Gospel). 1 Timothy 5:18 later quotes the same saying alongside Deut 25:4 AS 'scripture.' A second clear case (with IV.4-b) of Paul transmitting dominical tradition, and of an agraphon hardening into cited Scripture. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the seventy(-two) nations (Genesis 10, 70 MT / 72 LXX); the seventy elders of Moses (Numbers 11:16-25)
references.note: The number of the wider mission is symbolic and its textual variant (seventy vs. seventy-two) tracks a known scriptural split: the table of nations in Genesis 10 totals seventy in the MT, seventy-two in the LXX -- so the sending prefigures a mission to all the nations of the world. Secondarily it echoes the seventy elders on whom Moses's spirit rested (Num 11:16-25). Probable; the variant itself is the clue.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 14:12 (the fall of the Day Star); Psalm 91:13 (treading on serpent and asp)
references.note: 'I watched Satan fall like lightning from heaven' draws on the fall of the shining one, Isaiah 14:12 (the Day Star/Helel cast down), read as the defeat of the satanic power. 'Authority to tread on serpents and scorpions' is Psalm 91:13 ('you will tread on the lion and the asp') -- the same Psalm 91 the tempter weaponized at I.3-c, now turned to the disciples' protection. A pointed reversal of that earlier scene. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Esther 5:3,6; 7:2 ('up to half my kingdom'); Elijah vs. Jezebel/Ahab (1 Kgs 19:1-2; 21); Josephus, Ant. 18.116-119
references.note: The banquet-oath -- Herod's 'whatever you ask, up to half my kingdom' -- echoes Ahasuerus's identical promise to Esther (Esther 5:3,6; 7:2), casting the scene in the mold of a court tale. The deeper frame is Elijah persecuted by a murderous queen: Herodias plays Jezebel to John's Elijah, just as Jezebel sought Elijah's life (1 Kgs 19:1-2; 21), reinforcing the John-as-Elijah identification (I.1-c, V.3-c). Josephus independently reports John's execution by Antipas, though for political fear and at Machaerus (Ant. 18.116-119) -- an external control on the event behind Mark's court-tale shaping. Probable.
scholarship: on the Esther echo: Aus, Water into Wine and the Beheading of John the Baptist

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16; Ps 78:24-25); Elisha feeds a hundred (2 Kings 4:42-44); 'sheep without a shepherd' (Numbers 27:17; Ezek 34)
references.note: The wilderness feeding layers three OT streams. (i) Manna: bread given in the desert (Exod 16; Ps 78:24-25), making Jesus the new Moses provisioning Israel. (ii) Elisha: 2 Kings 4:42-44, where the prophet feeds a hundred from twenty loaves with food LEFT OVER -- the surplus motif (twelve baskets) is the signature of the Elisha typology. (iii) Shepherd: the crowds are 'like sheep without a shepherd' (Mark 6:34), quoting Numbers 27:17 (and evoking Ezek 34's promise that God will shepherd his flock), so the feeding answers Israel's leaderless condition. The only miracle in all four Gospels. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: God treads the sea (Job 9:8; Ps 77:19; Hab 3:15); the theophanic 'passing by' (Exod 33:19-23; 1 Kgs 19:11); 'I am' (egO eimi; Exod 3:14; Isa 43:10-13)
references.note: A compressed theophany. Walking on the sea is a divine act: God 'alone treads on the waves of the sea' (Job 9:8; cf. Ps 77:19, 'your way was through the sea'; Hab 3:15). 'He meant to PASS BY them' (6:48) is the technical language of theophany -- God 'passes by' Moses and Elijah on the mountain (Exod 33:19-23; 1 Kgs 19:11). And his word 'egO eimi -- it is I / I AM' (6:50) carries the divine self-identification of Exod 3:14 and Isaiah's 'I am he' (43:10-13). Three independent markers converge on a single claim. Established.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 6:45-52 and 'the epiphany on the sea'

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the fringe (kraspedon = tzitzit, Numbers 15:38-39); 'healing in its wings/kanaf' (Malachi 4:2)
references.note: The sick beg to touch 'the fringe of his garment' -- the kraspedon, the tzitzit tassel commanded in Numbers 15:38-39. The Hebrew kanaf means both 'corner/fringe' and 'wing,' so the healing-by-the-fringe may quietly evoke Malachi 4:2, the sun of righteousness with 'healing in its wings.' A brief, suggestive echo; possible.

VII.11.placement_flag: Peter's Johannine confession (6:66-71) cross-refs Caesarea Philippi (Part VIII).

references.speaker: other
references.source: Psalm 78:24-25 (+ Exodus 16:4, 15; Nehemiah 9:15): 'he gave them bread from heaven to eat'
references.note: The crowd quotes 'he gave them bread from heaven to eat' -- a composite of Psalm 78:24 and Exodus 16:4/15 (cf. Neh 9:15) -- and Jesus then expounds it midrashically: not Moses but the Father gives the true bread; 'I AM the bread of life.' The discourse follows a synagogue-homily pattern, citing the manna text and re-reading each phrase. Established.
scholarship: Borgen, Bread from Heaven (the homiletic structure)
Menken, OT Quotations in the Fourth Gospel, on 6:31

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Wisdom's banquet (Proverbs 9:5; Sirach 24:19-21); manna-as-Torah/word tradition
references.note: 'I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me will never hunger' speaks in the idiom of personified Wisdom inviting to her table -- 'come, eat of my bread' (Prov 9:5), 'those who eat me will hunger for more' (Sir 24:19-21) -- and engages the contemporary reading of manna as Torah/wisdom/word (Philo; the rabbis). Jesus presents himself as the true bread these traditions anticipated. The eat-my-flesh intensification pushes the Wisdom-banquet motif to a scandalous edge. Probable.

VII.12.canon_title: Tradition of the elders; clean and unclean

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 29:13 (LXX form)
references.note: 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines' quotes Isaiah 29:13 -- and the argument DEPENDS on the LXX: the clinching line 'teaching as doctrines the commandments of men' renders the Greek, where the Hebrew reads differently ('their fear of me is a commandment of men learned by rote'). The polemic against tradition-as-doctrine works on the Greek text. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Corban / vow-dedication (Lev 27; Num 30; cf. m. Nedarim); the narrator's gloss 'cleansing all foods' vs. Leviticus 11
references.note: Two background points. 'Corban' (qorban, a gift devoted to God, Lev 27; Num 30) names the vow by which property could be withheld from needy parents -- the case Jesus uses against elevating tradition over the commandment to honor father and mother. More consequentially, Mark adds the editorial parenthesis 'thus he declared all foods clean' (7:19) -- a NARRATORIAL interpretation abrogating the kashrut of Leviticus 11. Flag (your kernel/overlay distinction): whether Jesus intended to void the food laws or whether this is Mark's later, possibly Pauline-influenced inference is debated; Matthew notably DROPS the parenthesis. Logged as the evangelist's framing, not a dominical citation.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 7:19 (the crux of the parenthesis)
on Corban: m. Nedarim; Marcus ad loc.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: 'dogs' as epithet for Gentiles; 'lost sheep of Israel' (Jer 50:6; Ezek 34); the Sidon setting (cf. 1 Kgs 17, the Sidonian widow)
references.note: The exchange runs on the Israel-first boundary: the 'children's bread' must not be thrown to the 'dogs,' using the standard Jewish epithet for Gentiles. Matthew sharpens it with 'I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (15:24), the shepherd-and-scattered-flock image of Jer 50:6 and Ezek 34. The setting is the region of Tyre and Sidon -- the same Gentile territory of the Sidonian widow Elijah was sent to (1 Kgs 17; cf. II.9-d), so a Gentile woman's faith again pries open the boundary. The woman's retort wins the exception. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 35:5-6 (deaf hear, mute sing); 'he has done all things well' echoing Genesis 1:31
references.note: The deaf-mute's cure enacts Isaiah 35:5-6 -- 'the ears of the deaf unstopped... the tongue of the mute sing' -- the same messianic-restoration text behind Jesus's answer to John (V.3-a). The crowd's acclamation 'he has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak' echoes the creation refrain 'God saw that it was very good' (Gen 1:31), framing the healing as new creation. 'Ephphatha' preserves the Aramaic. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: doublet of the five thousand (VII.8); same manna/Elisha background, now in Gentile territory (the Decapolis)
references.note: The second feeding repeats the manna-and-Elisha pattern of VII.8 but is set in the Gentile Decapolis -- bread now broken for the nations, the counterpart to the Jewish feeding (the seven baskets are sometimes read for the seventy nations; cf. VII.6-a). Mark himself treats the two as distinct events (8:19-20). Cross-ref VII.8. Probable.

VII.16.canon_title: Demand for a sign; leaven of the Pharisees

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-refs: the sign of Jonah (V.10) and leaven-as-corruption (VI.5-a)
references.note: Two threads already in the apparatus reconverge. 'No sign will be given to this generation' restates the sign refusal of V.10 (Matthew adds the Jonah exception at 16:4). 'Beware the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod' uses leaven in its standard NEGATIVE sense -- pervasive corrupting influence -- the inverse of the kingdom-leaven of VI.5-a, confirming that the symbol's polarity is context-set. Established as cross-references.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: opening-blind-eyes (Isa 35:5; 29:18; 42:7); the two-stage healing as narrative symbol
references.note: The cure of blindness invokes the same Isaianic restoration cluster as V.3-a / VII.14 (Isa 35:5; 29:18; 42:7). Distinctive to Mark is the TWO-STAGE healing (men like trees, then clear sight) -- unique in the Gospels and placed deliberately: it mirrors the disciples' half-seeing, bridging their incomprehension (8:21) to Peter's partial confession that follows (8:29). The structure is the message. Probable.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 8:22-26 (the two-stage healing and Markan structure)

references.speaker: other
references.source: prophet-redivivus expectation (Elijah, Mal 4:5; the eschatological prophet, Deut 18:15); Christos = Mashiach
references.note: The opinion-poll -- John raised, Elijah, 'one of the prophets' -- maps the live first-century menu of returning-figure expectations (Elijah of Mal 4:5; a prophet like Moses, Deut 18:15). Peter's answer, 'you are the Anointed' (Christos = Hebrew Mashiach; rendered 'Anointed' per policy), names the royal-messianic category the crowd's guesses circle. Established.
scholarship: Collins, The Scepter and the Star (messianic expectations)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 22:22 (the key of the house of David, to open and shut); binding-and-loosing (rabbinic asar/hittir); 'gates of Hades' and the Paneas setting
references.note: Matthew's special material gives Peter 'the keys of the kingdom,' alluding to Isaiah 22:22, where the key of the house of David is laid on Eliakim's shoulder -- the steward who 'opens and none shall shut.' 'Binding and loosing' is the rabbinic idiom for authoritative legal decision (to forbid/permit). The 'gates of Hades' gain extra edge from the setting: Caesarea Philippi (Paneas) stood at a great cave-mouth sacred to Pan, locally reputed an entrance to the underworld. Established for Isa 22:22; the Paneas resonance is historical-cultural color.
scholarship: Isa 22:22; on binding/loosing: Str-B with dating caution

VIII.2.canon_title: First passion prediction; taking up the cross

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the rejected stone (Psalm 118:22); the suffering righteous one (Isa 53; Wis 2-5; Ps 22); 'after three days' (Hosea 6:2)
references.note: 'The son of humanity must suffer many things and be REJECTED by the elders' uses the verb (apodokimazO) of Psalm 118:22, the stone the builders rejected -- a psalm Jesus will cite outright at the vineyard parable (Part X) and that frames the passion. The pattern of the suffering-then-vindicated righteous one draws on Isaiah 53, Wisdom 2-5, and Psalm 22. 'After three days he will rise' may echo Hosea 6:2 ('on the third day he will raise us up'). Probable; the 'must' (dei) signals scriptural necessity without naming a single text.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 8:31 and The Way of the Lord

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:13-14 (the son of man coming in glory); the priceless life/soul (Ps 49:7-9); psychE
references.note: 'Whoever is ashamed of me... the son of humanity will be ashamed of, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels' draws on Daniel 7:13-14, the coming son of man given dominion. The saying on gaining the world but forfeiting one's psychE (life/self/soul -- glossary) echoes the wisdom that no wealth can ransom a life (Ps 49:7-9). 'Take up the cross' presupposes the Roman practice of the condemned carrying the crossbar. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the Sinai theophany: 'after six days' (Exod 24:16); the high mountain; the shining (Exod 34:29-35); the overshadowing cloud (Exod 24:15-18; 40:34-38)
references.note: The scene is built from Sinai. 'After six days' replays Exod 24:16, where the glory settles on the mountain six days before God calls Moses on the seventh; the high mountain is Sinai/Horeb; the transfigured radiance answers Moses's shining face (Exod 34:29-35); the cloud that overshadows and the voice from it are the Shekinah-cloud of Exod 24:15-18 and 40:34-38. Moses AND Elijah appear -- the two who met God on that mountain (Exod; 1 Kgs 19), each with a mysterious end -- and Peter's instinct to build three booths (skEnai) reaches for Tabernacles. Jesus is staged as the new and greater Sinai. Established.

references.speaker: other
references.source: Deuteronomy 18:15 ('listen to him'); Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 42:1 (cf. the baptism, I.2-b)
references.note: The voice -- 'This is my son, the beloved; LISTEN TO HIM' -- repeats the baptismal fusion of Psalm 2:7 ('my son') and Isaiah 42:1 ('the beloved/chosen,' I.2-b) and ADDS the climactic 'listen to him,' which is Deuteronomy 18:15: the prophet like Moses whom God will raise up, 'him you shall heed.' So the Sinai tableau resolves into a command to obey Jesus as the awaited Mosaic prophet, with Moses and Elijah (Law and Prophets) deferring to him. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Malachi 4:5-6 [MT 3:23-24] (Elijah must come first); the suffering son of man
references.note: Descending, they debate the scribal teaching that 'Elijah must come first' -- Malachi 4:5-6 -- and Jesus affirms it while reapplying it: 'Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they wished,' i.e. John (cf. I.1-c, V.3-c, and John's death VII.7). He couples it with the harder question, 'how is it written that the son of humanity should suffer many things?' -- pairing the Elijah-forerunner schedule with the suffering-Messiah necessity. Established.

VIII.4.canon_title: The boy with an unclean spirit

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Deuteronomy 32:5,20 (the faithless, perverse generation)
references.note: 'O faithless generation, how long must I bear with you?' echoes the Song of Moses, where Israel is 'a perverse and crooked generation,' 'children in whom there is no faithfulness' (Deut 32:5, 20). The wilderness generation's faithlessness is laid over the disciples' inability to cast out the spirit; the pericope's pivot is pistis ('all things are possible to the one who trusts' -- 'I trust; help my untrust'). Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 53:6,12 LXX ('handed over,' paradidOmi)
references.note: 'The son of humanity is being HANDED OVER (paradidotai) into human hands' uses the verb the LXX of Isaiah 53:6,12 applies to the Servant who 'was handed over for our sins.' The passive hints at divine agency behind the betrayal. Brief; cross-ref the passion-prediction series (VIII.2, and onward). Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the half-shekel temple tax (Exodus 30:11-16, the census atonement-money)
references.note: The 'two-drachma' collectors are gathering the annual half-shekel temple tax instituted in Exodus 30:11-16 as 'ransom for the life' at the census. Jesus's logic -- kings tax strangers, not their own sons, so 'the sons are free' -- implies the Son's exemption from the Father's house, while paying it anyway 'not to give offense.' The coin-in-the-fish is a distinct wonder-motif. Historical-cultural background essential to the point. Established.

VIII.7.canon_title: Who is the greatest; the child

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: status-reversal (the least/servant as greatest); the child as the lowliest; the agent/shaliach principle ('whoever receives the sender')
references.note: 'Whoever would be first must be last and servant of all,' and the placing of a child (a person of no social standing) at the center, enact the great-reversal that runs through the canon (the Beatitudes, the Magnificat). 'Whoever receives one such child receives me, and the one who sent me' applies the agency principle (the shaliach -- the one sent carries the sender's authority/identity). Tradition-motif; probable.
scholarship: on the shaliach principle: m. Berakhot 5:5 (with dating caution)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Numbers 11:26-29 (Eldad and Medad; Moses rebukes Joshua's jealousy for unauthorized prophesying)
references.note: John's complaint -- an outsider casting out demons in Jesus's name, 'we tried to stop him' -- and Jesus's 'do not stop him... whoever is not against us is for us' replays Numbers 11:26-29, where Joshua wants Moses to silence Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp, and Moses answers, 'would that all the LORD's people were prophets!' Jesus takes the magnanimous Moses-role against the disciple's Joshua-jealousy. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 66:24 (the undying worm, the unquenched fire) -- the last verse of Isaiah
references.note: 'Gehenna, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched' quotes the closing verse of Isaiah (66:24), the dead rebels whose corpses are a perpetual horror. Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (cf. IV.3-b), here the image of final judgment. A direct citation, thrice repeated in Mark's fullest form. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the covenant of salt (Lev 2:13; Num 18:19); cf. the salt saying at IV.2
references.note: 'Everyone will be salted with fire... have salt in yourselves' draws on salt's double freight: the salt of the sacrificial/covenant offering (Lev 2:13, 'the salt of the covenant'; Num 18:19) and the salt-saying already met at IV.2. The 'salted with fire' line is famously obscure; the covenant-salt and purifying-fire associations are the available background. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Ezekiel 34:6,11-16 (God seeks the lost/strayed sheep); non-canonical parallel Thomas 107
references.note: The shepherd leaving the ninety-nine to seek the one strayed sheep enacts Ezekiel 34, where God himself promises to 'seek the lost, bring back the strayed' (34:6,11-16) against the failed shepherds of Israel. Independently attested at Thomas 107 -- where the lost sheep is the LARGEST, a divergent valuation worth flagging. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 107

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Genesis 4:24 (Lamech's seventy-sevenfold vengeance) -- inverted
references.note: SHOWCASE inversion. 'Not seven times, but seventy times seven' deliberately reverses Lamech's boast in Genesis 4:24: 'if Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold.' Jesus takes the archetypal escalation of vengeance and turns the very number into the measure of FORGIVENESS. The clearest single case of a text cited to be stood on its head -- precisely the kind of pointed reversal that marks the distinctive teaching against its background. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the reproof procedure: Leviticus 19:17; the two-or-three witnesses (Deut 19:15); Qumran community discipline (1QS 5:24-6:1; CD 9:2-8)
references.note: The graduated discipline -- reprove privately, then before witnesses, then before the assembly -- codifies Leviticus 19:17 ('you shall surely reprove your neighbor') with the Deuteronomic two-or-three-witnesses rule (Deut 19:15). The closest contemporary analogue is the Qumran reproof procedure (1QS 5:24-6:1; CD 9:2-8), which legislates the same private-then-public steps. Jesus's community order sits within an existing Jewish disciplinary form. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: sin-as-debt and forgiveness-as-release (cf. IV.6-b, the Lord's Prayer); measure-for-measure judgment
references.note: The parable literalizes the debt-metaphor for sin that the Lord's Prayer assumes (IV.6-b): the servant forgiven an unpayable debt (ten thousand talents) who then throttles a fellow over a trifle (a hundred denarii). The reciprocal logic -- forgiven must forgive, or the remission is revoked -- is the measure-for-measure principle (cf. IV.8-a, VI.2-b) applied to mercy. Established as the controlling motif.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Elijah cycle: 2 Kings 1:10-12 (fire from heaven); 1 Kings 19:19-21 (Elisha's farewell, the plow); 'set his face' (Isaiah 50:7)
references.note: The travel narrative opens steeped in Elijah. Jesus 'set his face' to go to Jerusalem -- Isaiah 50:7, the Servant who set his face 'like flint.' When the Samaritan village refuses him, James and John want to 'call down fire from heaven,' exactly Elijah's act against the soldiers (2 Kgs 1:10-12) -- and Jesus REBUKES them, an anti-Elijah. Then the would-be follower asks to bid family farewell, replaying Elisha's request to kiss his parents before following (1 Kgs 19:19-21), but Jesus is harsher than Elijah was: 'no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back' -- Elisha's very plow. Jesus invokes the Elijah-Elisha call only to outbid it. Established.

references.speaker: other
references.source: Deuteronomy 6:5 + Leviticus 19:18 (love God and neighbor); cross-ref the greatest-commandment, Part X
references.note: The lawyer's summary of the law fuses Deuteronomy 6:5 (love YHWH with all heart, soul, strength) and Leviticus 19:18 (love your neighbor) -- the same pairing Jesus gives as the two great commandments (handled at Part X, the structural keystone of the canon). The parable then answers 'who is my neighbor?' by redefining the neighbor as the one who acts. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: priestly corpse-impurity (Lev 21:1-4; Num 19:11-16); Samaritan-Jewish enmity; the OT precedent of 2 Chronicles 28:15
references.note: The priest and Levite who pass by may be guarding against corpse-impurity (Lev 21:1-4; Num 19) on the bandit-ridden Jerusalem-to-Jericho descent -- duty weaponized into neglect. The hero is the despised Samaritan (cf. IX.1; Gerizim, II.6-c). A striking and rarely-noted OT precedent stands behind the choice: in 2 Chronicles 28:15 it is SAMARITANS (men of the north) who clothe, feed, anoint, and carry Judean captives on donkeys 'to Jericho' -- the parable's exact geography and acts of mercy. Probable that 2 Chr 28 supplies the template.
scholarship: 2 Chr 28:15 (the parallel proposed by Spencer and others)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: 'sitting at the feet' as the disciple's posture (cf. Acts 22:3, at the feet of Gamaliel)
references.note: Mary 'sat at the Lord's feet and listened' -- the technical posture of the disciple under a teacher (Paul was schooled 'at the feet of Gamaliel,' Acts 22:3). That a WOMAN takes the disciple's place, commended over domestic service, is the quiet reversal. Otherwise a domestic scene, light on allusion. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the obligation of night hospitality; anaideia (shameless persistence)
references.note: The midnight request for loaves trades on the binding duty of hospitality to a traveler and the social shame (anaideia) of failing it -- the householder rises 'because of his shamelessness.' Cultural background to a prayer-parable; light on intertext. Possible.

IX.5.canon_title: Woes against the Pharisees and lawyers
IX.5.placement_flag: Grouped with Matthew 23 at Part X, where the woes are treated in full (tithing herbs vs. justice; whitewashed tombs; the blood of Abel to Zechariah, Gen 4:8 + 2 Chr 24:20-22).

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-ref Part X: 'blood of Abel' (Gen 4:8) to 'blood of Zechariah' (2 Chr 24:20-22)
references.note: Pointer entry. The climactic 'from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah' spans the Hebrew canon from its first murder (Gen 4:8) to its last (2 Chr 24:20-22, Chronicles being the last book in the Jewish order) -- a whole-Bible inclusio of martyred prophets. Full treatment with the Matthew 23 woes at Part X. Established.

IX.6.canon_title: Fear God; confess Christ; the unforgivable word

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-refs: hidden/revealed (VI.2-a); the son of man confessing before the angels (Dan 7:13-14); blasphemy against the Spirit (V.8)
references.note: A cluster of sayings already in the apparatus: 'nothing covered that will not be revealed' (cf. VI.2-a / Thomas 5-6); confessing-and-being-confessed before the angels invokes the Danielic son of man (Dan 7); and the unforgivable word against the Spirit cross-refs the Beelzebul charge (V.8). The sparrows-and-hairs assurance is sapiential providence (cf. IV.7-d). Probable as cross-references.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel Thomas 63 (and P.Oxy 5575); Sirach 11:18-19 (the rich man who says 'I have found rest' then dies); Ps 49:16-20; Eccl 2
references.note: The rich fool is independently attested at Thomas 63, and its ending is now also attested in Greek at P.Oxy 5575 (freshness flag as at IV.7-c). The man's self-talk -- 'you have ample goods, relax, eat, drink, be merry' -- closely tracks Sirach 11:18-19, where the man who says 'I have found rest, now I will enjoy my goods' does not know his hour is coming; with the futility-of-hoarded-wealth of Psalm 49 and Ecclesiastes. 'This night your life (psychE) is demanded of you' answers the boast. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 63

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: loins girded, lamps lit (Exodus 12:11, Passover readiness); the thief in the night
references.note: 'Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,' waiting for the master's return, echoes the Passover posture of readiness for sudden departure (Exod 12:11, eaten 'with loins girded'). The thief-in-the-night image becomes a fixed eschatological figure (1 Thess 5:2; Rev 16:15). Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Micah 7:6 (son against father, daughter against mother, foes of one's own household)
references.note: 'I came not to bring peace but division... father against son... mother against daughter' quotes Micah 7:6, the prophet's picture of social collapse where one's enemies are one's own household. In Micah it is a lament; Jesus makes it the predicted cost of allegiance to him. Established (also at Matt 10:35-36).

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the fig tree / vineyard as Israel under judgment (Isa 5:1-7; Jer 8:13; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1)
references.note: The unfruitful fig tree spared one more year draws on the prophetic figure of Israel as the vine/fig that yields no fruit and faces the axe (Isa 5:1-7; Jer 8:13; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1). The Pilate/Siloam sayings that precede it (13:1-5) reflect real events (cf. Josephus on Pilate). The fig-as-Israel link prepares the cursed fig tree of the final week (Part X). Probable.

IX.11.canon_title: Healing the bent woman on the Sabbath

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the Sabbath life-saving/animal-care debate (cf. III.9-a; CD 11:13-17); 'daughter of Abraham'
references.note: Jesus's defense -- you untie your ox or donkey to water it on the Sabbath, so may not this 'daughter of Abraham, bound by Satan eighteen years,' be loosed? -- argues a fortiori from the conceded permission to tend animals (the very case Qumran forbade, CD 11:13-17), squarely inside the Sabbath halakhah of III.9-a. 'Daughter of Abraham' asserts her covenant standing. Established.

IX.12.canon_title: The narrow door; lament over Jerusalem

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 6:8 ('depart from me, workers of iniquity'); the banquet from east and west (cf. V.1-a; Ps 107:3)
references.note: The narrow-door warning closes with 'depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' (Psalm 6:8) and the in-gathering 'from east and west, north and south' to recline in the kingdom with the patriarchs -- the eschatological banquet and Gentile inclusion already at V.1-a (Ps 107:3; Isa 25:6). The reversal: insiders shut out, outsiders seated. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 118:26 ('blessed is the one coming in the name of YHWH'); Deuteronomy 32:11 + Ps 36:7 (wings); Jeremiah 12:7; 22:5 (forsaken house)
references.note: The lament over Jerusalem layers three references in a few lines. (a) QUOTATION of Psalm 118:26 (LXX 117:26), verbatim, 'blessed is the one coming in the name of YHWH' -- anarthrous Kyrios, hence YHWH; the same verse acclaims the Triumphal Entry (Part X), making this its setup. (b) ALLUSION in 'as a hen gathers her brood under her wings' to the wing-shelter topos (Deut 32:11, the eagle over its young; Ps 36:7; Ruth 2:12); the same image recurs in 5 Ezra (2 Esdras 1:30) -- flagged as a LATER Christian source dependent on this tradition, not a source for it. (c) ECHO of the abandoned-temple oracle in 'your house is left to you [desolate]' (Jer 12:7; 22:5; cf. 1 Kgs 9:7-8). Established; the foundational worked example of the apparatus.

IX.13.canon_title: At a Pharisee's table; places of honor; the great banquet

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Proverbs 25:6-7 ('do not put yourself forward before the king; better to be told come up here')
references.note: The counsel on choosing the lowest place, lest one be demoted before the company, versifies Proverbs 25:6-7 nearly directly -- 'do not put yourself forward in the king's presence... it is better to be told come up here than to be put lower.' Jesus turns table-etiquette into the great-reversal maxim, 'all who exalt themselves will be humbled.' Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel Thomas 64; the eschatological banquet (Isa 25:6); inversion of the Qumran exclusion of the disabled (1QSa 2:5-22; cf. Lev 21:17-23)
references.note: The great banquet with its excuses is independently attested at Thomas 64 (which ends with the sting 'buyers and merchants will not enter'). It draws on the eschatological feast (Isa 25:6), but the guest list is a pointed INVERSION: the host fills the table with 'the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame' -- precisely the categories the Qumran Rule of the Congregation BARS from the eschatological assembly (1QSa 2:5-22, excluding the lame, blind, and deaf, on the logic of Lev 21:17-23). Where the sectarians fence the messianic banquet against the disabled, Jesus seats them first. A first-rank zeitgeist datapoint and a sharp divergence. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 64

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallels Thomas 55 and 101 ('hate father and mother'); cf. Deuteronomy 33:9 (Levi disregards kin)
references.note: 'Whoever does not hate father and mother... cannot be my disciple' is independently attested at Thomas 55 and 101, with the cross-bearing demand attached. The Semitic 'hate' is comparative ('love less'), and the renunciation of kin for a higher loyalty recalls Deuteronomy 33:9, where Levi disregards parents and children for the covenant (cf. V.11-a). The closing salt-saying (14:34-35) cross-refs IV.2 and VIII.9-b. The renunciation-of-the-world theme also draws in Thomas 27 / P.Oxy 5575 ('fast from the world'). Established.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 55, 101

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the seeking-and-finding of the lost (Ezekiel 34, cf. VIII.10-a); 'dead and alive again, lost and found' as restoration
references.note: The lost coin completes the lost-sheep/lost-son triad of seeking the strayed (Ezek 34; cf. VIII.10-a). The prodigal carries no single citation but runs on the refrain 'he was dead and is alive again, lost and found' -- restoration language -- and the younger-son/elder-son rivalry resonates with the Jacob/Esau and Joseph cycles, with the elder brother often read as the resentful insider (Israel/the righteous). Mostly motif; probable.
scholarship: Bailey, Poet and Peasant (the cultural reading)

IX.16.canon_title: The dishonest manager; the law; the rich man and Lazarus

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-ref: 'no servant can serve two masters... God and mammon' (IV.7-b; Thomas 47)
references.note: The dishonest-manager parable closes with the two-masters saying already logged at IV.7-b (Thomas 47). Cross-reference. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the afterlife reversal-of-fortunes folktale: the Egyptian demotic tale of Setne/Si-Osiris; the rabbinic bar Ma'yan tale (y. Hagigah 2:2; y. Sanhedrin 6:6); 'Abraham's bosom'
references.note: ZEITGEIST showcase. The rich man and Lazarus deploys a migratory folktale of reversed fortunes in the next world: the Egyptian demotic story of Setne Khamwas and his son Si-Osiris (a rich man buried in splendor tormented below, a poor man honored) is the oldest form, and a Jewish version circulated about the tax-collector bar Ma'yan and a poor scholar (preserved in the Palestinian Talmud). The tale was available in the first-century Mediterranean; Jesus adapts it, adding the sting that 'they have Moses and the prophets' and 'neither will they be convinced if someone rises from the dead.' Direction: the Egyptian source predates; the Jewish parallels are roughly contemporary/later. 'Abraham's bosom' is the place of the righteous dead. Probable.
scholarship: Hock, 'Lazarus and Micyllus: Greco-Roman Backgrounds to Luke 16:19-31,' JBL 106 (1987)
Bauckham, 'The Rich Man and Lazarus: The Parable and the Parallels,' NTS 37 (1991)

IX.17.canon_title: Faith, duty, and the ten lepers

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: leprosy purification (Lev 13-14, cf. III.4-a); Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5, the foreigner cleansed who returns); the Samaritan (cf. IX.2)
references.note: 'Show yourselves to the priests' invokes the Levitical cleansing rite (Lev 13-14; cf. III.4-a). The one who returns to give thanks is a SAMARITAN (cf. IX.1-2, II.6) -- a foreigner, like Naaman the Syrian, the leper whose cleansing and grateful return (2 Kgs 5) Jesus had already cited at Nazareth (II.9-d). The outsider's gratitude indicts the nine. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallels Thomas 113 and 3 ('the kingdom is spread out / within you')
references.note: 'The kingdom of God is not coming with signs to be observed... the kingdom of God is entos hymOn' is independently paralleled at Thomas 113 ('the kingdom is spread out upon the earth and people do not see it') and Thomas 3 ('the kingdom is inside you and outside you'). The Greek entos hymOn is a standing lexical crux -- 'within you' (interior) or 'among/in the midst of you' (already present in Jesus); the Thomas parallels lean toward the spatial/present sense rather than the purely interior. Flagged for the lexical layer; established as a parallel.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 3, 113
Fitzmyer, AYB Luke, on 17:20-21 (the entos crux)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the days of Noah (Genesis 6-7) and of Lot (Genesis 19); 'remember Lot's wife' (Gen 19:26)
references.note: The suddenness of the day is figured by the flood (Gen 6-7) and the destruction of Sodom (Gen 19): people eating, marrying, buying, building until catastrophe falls 'on the day Lot went out.' 'Remember Lot's wife' (Gen 19:26, turned to a pillar of salt for looking back) warns against looking back like the would-be follower of IX.1. Established.

IX.19.canon_title: The persistent widow; the Pharisee and tax collector

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: God vindicates the widow (Sirach 35:14-19; Exod 22:22-24); the penitent's prayer (Psalm 51:1)
references.note: The widow who wins justice from the unjust judge trades on the OT conviction that God hears the widow's cry and will not delay her vindication (Sir 35:14-19; Exod 22:22-24). The tax collector's 'God, be merciful to me, the sinner' echoes the penitential idiom of Psalm 51:1, and the parable closes on the reversal 'all who exalt themselves will be humbled' (cf. IX.13-a). Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the Sukkot water-libation; 'rivers of living water' (Zech 14:8; Isa 12:3; 58:11; Ezek 47:1-12; Prov 18:4)
references.note: On the last day of Tabernacles -- whose central rite was the daily water-libation, water drawn from Siloam and poured at the altar -- Jesus cries 'let the thirsty come to me... out of his heart shall flow rivers of living water, as the scripture says.' No single text matches verbatim; it is a composite of the eschatological living-waters from Jerusalem/the temple (Zech 14:8; Ezek 47:1-12; Isa 12:3; 58:11). Continues the living-water thread of II.6-b. The festival setting is the key. Established.
scholarship: on the Sukkot libation: m. Sukkah 4-5

IX.21.canon_title: I am the light of the world; the controversies

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the Sukkot temple-illumination; light imagery (Isa 9:2; 42:6; 49:6; 60:1-3; Ps 27:1)
references.note: 'I am the light of the world' is spoken at Tabernacles, whose other great rite was the nightly illumination of the Court of the Women by giant menorahs said to light all Jerusalem. Against that backdrop Jesus claims the light-imagery of Isaiah's servant-light to the nations (42:6; 49:6; 60:1-3) and the dawning light of 9:2. The festival lamps are the occasion. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Exodus 3:14 ('I AM'); Isaiah 43:10-13 ('I am he')
references.note: 'Before Abraham was, egO eimi -- I AM' claims the divine self-designation of Exodus 3:14 and the Isaianic 'I am he' (43:10-13), which is why the hearers immediately take up stones. The absolute egO eimi (no predicate) is the Johannine signature of the divine name, met already on the sea (VII.9-a). Established.
scholarship: Brown, AYB John, on 8:58 and Appendix IV (the 'I AM' sayings)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the sin-and-suffering question (Exod 20:5 vs Ezek 18:20); clay and breath (Gen 2:7); Siloam = 'Sent'; opening blind eyes (Isa 35:5; 42:7)
references.note: 'Who sinned, this man or his parents?' poses the visiting-of-iniquity principle (Exod 20:5) against the individual-responsibility correction (Ezek 18:20); Jesus refuses both. Making clay from spittle to open the eyes recalls the forming of the human from clay (Gen 2:7) -- a new-creation overtone, since 'never has anyone opened the eyes of one born blind' (9:32). John glosses Siloam as 'Sent' (the one sent washes in the pool called Sent). The cure continues the Isaianic blindness-opening (Isa 35:5; 42:7; cf. V.3-a). Probable.

IX.23.canon_title: The Good Shepherd; the Feast of Dedication

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Ezekiel 34 (false shepherds vs. God the true shepherd); Psalm 23; Isaiah 40:11; Zechariah 11; 13:7
references.note: The Good Shepherd discourse is built on Ezekiel 34: the worthless shepherds who feed themselves and scatter the flock, against YHWH who will himself seek, gather, and shepherd his sheep -- and set over them 'one shepherd, my servant David' (Ezek 34:23). Behind it stand Psalm 23, the gentle shepherd of Isaiah 40:11, and the smitten shepherd of Zechariah 11 / 13:7. 'I lay down my life for the sheep' is the divergence: the shepherd who dies for the flock. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 82:6 ('I said, you are gods'); the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) setting
references.note: At the Feast of Dedication, charged with making himself God, Jesus cites Psalm 82:6 -- 'I said, you are gods' -- arguing from the lesser to the greater: if scripture can call the recipients of God's word 'gods,' the charge of blasphemy fails on its own legal premises. A rabbinic-style qal wahomer argument from the written text. The Dedication (Hanukkah) commemorates the Maccabean rededication of the altar. Established.
scholarship: on the argument: Neyrey, 'I Said: You Are Gods,' JBL 108 (1989)

IX.24.canon_title: The raising of Lazarus; the plot

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: resurrection hope (Daniel 12:2); Ezekiel 37:12-13 ('I will open your graves'); Elijah/Elisha raisings
references.note: 'I am the resurrection and the life' engages the Jewish hope of resurrection 'on the last day' (Martha's confession, 11:24), grounded in Daniel 12:2. The command 'Lazarus, come out,' calling the dead from the tomb, enacts Ezekiel 37's promise 'I will open your graves and raise you' and joins the prophetic raising-pattern (Elijah, Elisha; cf. V.2-a, VII.3-b). The four-days-dead stresses irreversibility. Probable.

references.speaker: other
references.source: the unwitting prophecy of the high priest (Caiaphas)
references.note: Caiaphas's cynical counsel -- 'better that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish' -- the narrator reads as unwitting prophecy spoken by virtue of the high-priestly office (a Johannine irony, trading on the belief that the high priest could prophesy). Tradition-motif; probable.

IX.25.placement_flag: Fully treated at IV.4 (the antithesis on divorce). This Synoptic debate-form is the same teaching; see IV.4-a (Gen 1:27/2:24 over Deut 24:1; CD 4:20-5:2) and IV.4-b (1 Cor 7:10-11).

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-ref IV.4-a: Genesis 1:27 + 2:24 over Deuteronomy 24:1
references.note: The debate form -- 'is it lawful to divorce?' answered by setting creation (Gen 1:27; 2:24) above the Mosaic concession (Deut 24:1) -- is the same Scripture-against-Scripture move treated at IV.4-a, with its Qumran twin in CD 4:20-5:2. Cross-reference. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel Thomas 22 (entering as infants); the child as model of the kingdom (cf. VIII.7-a)
references.note: 'Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it' shares the children-and-kingdom motif independently developed at Thomas 22 ('the infants being suckled are like those who enter the kingdom'). The child models dependence and lack of status (cf. VIII.7-a), not innocence as moderns hear it. Probable.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 22

IX.27.canon_title: The rich young ruler; reward of discipleship

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the Decalogue, second table (Exodus 20:12-16 // Deuteronomy 5:16-20)
references.note: Jesus recites the second-table commandments -- do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, defraud, honor father and mother (Exod 20:12-16 // Deut 5:16-20). 'Do not defraud' substitutes for coveting; Matthew adds 'love your neighbor as yourself' (Lev 19:18). The man keeps them all, yet the one thing lacking exposes the hold of wealth. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the camel through the needle's eye (proverbial impossibility)
references.note: 'Easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom' is a deliberate hyperbole of impossibility (the largest local animal, the smallest aperture); a parallel rabbinic saying uses an elephant through a needle's eye. The medieval 'Needle Gate' explanation is unfounded -- the point is sheer impossibility apart from God. Probable as proverbial form.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the vineyard as Israel (Isa 5:1-7); the 'evil eye' idiom for envy (20:15); the last-first reversal
references.note: The vineyard setting carries the standing figure of Israel as God's vineyard (Isa 5:1-7), though the parable's weight is on the owner's freedom to be generous. 'Is your eye evil because I am good?' uses the Semitic 'evil eye' idiom for envy/grudging. The frame 'the last will be first, and the first last' (cf. IX.27, the great reversal) brackets it. Probable.
scholarship: on the evil eye: BDAG s.v. ophthalmos

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 50:6 (the servant's back to the smiters, the spitting); cross-ref the passion-prediction series (VIII.2, VIII.5)
references.note: The fullest passion prediction adds the details of mocking, spitting, and flogging -- the treatment of the Servant in Isaiah 50:6, 'I gave my back to the smiters... I hid not my face from shame and spitting.' Completes the threefold prediction (VIII.2, VIII.5) with explicit Servant-suffering coloring. Probable.

IX.30.canon_title: The request of James and John; servant leadership

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the cup of wrath (Isaiah 51:17,22; Jeremiah 25:15-16; Psalm 75:8); the baptism-of-suffering
references.note: 'Can you drink the cup that I drink?' invokes the prophetic 'cup' of God's wrath/judgment that one is given to drink (Isa 51:17,22; Jer 25:15-16; Ps 75:8), here the cup of the passion Jesus will pray to have removed in Gethsemane (Part X). The paired 'baptism' is being overwhelmed in suffering. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 53:10-12 (the Servant's life as guilt-offering, bearing the sin of 'the many')
references.note: 'The son of humanity came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many (lytron anti pollOn)' is the clearest Servant-Song self-application in the canon. Isaiah 53 makes the Servant's life an asham (guilt-offering) who 'bore the sin of MANY (rabbim / hoi polloi)' and 'poured out his life to death' (53:10-12); the distinctive 'the many' tracks Isaiah's repeated 'the many.' The substitutionary 'for many' will return at the Last Supper (Part X). Established.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 10:45 and The Way of the Lord
Jeremias, NT Theology, on the ransom saying

references.speaker: other
references.source: 'Son of David' as messianic title (2 Sam 7:12-16; Isa 11:1; Ps 89); the Son-of-David-as-healer tradition; opening blind eyes (Isa 35:5)
references.note: Bartimaeus's cry 'Son of David, have mercy on me' invokes the Davidic-messianic hope (2 Sam 7; Isa 11:1; Ps 89), and possibly the contemporary tradition of Solomon, son of David, as exorcist-healer. The healing of blindness continues the Isaianic restoration (Isa 35:5; cf. V.3-a, VII.17-a), and Bartimaeus's following 'on the way' frames the entry to Jerusalem. Probable.
scholarship: on Son of David as healer: Duling, 'Solomon, Exorcism, and the Son of David'

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: restitution law (Exod 22:1; Lev 6:5; Num 5:7); 'the son of man came to seek and save the lost' (Ezekiel 34:16); 'son of Abraham'
references.note: Zacchaeus's fourfold restoration for fraud follows the Torah's restitution scale (Exod 22:1 fourfold for a stolen sheep; with Lev 6:5 / Num 5:7 adding a fifth for confessed wrong). Jesus's summary, 'the son of humanity came to SEEK and to SAVE the LOST,' quotes the shepherd-language of Ezekiel 34:16 ('I will seek the lost'), the keynote of the seeking-God parables (VIII.10, IX.15). 'Son of Abraham' restores the despised toll-collector to covenant standing. Established.

IX.33.canon_title: The parable of the pounds / talents

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the nobleman seeking a kingdom abroad (Archelaus's journey to Rome, opposed by a delegation, 4 BCE; Josephus, Ant. 17.299-320); 'to everyone who has, more given' (cf. VI.2-b)
references.note: Luke's frame -- a nobleman travels 'to a far country to receive kingly power and return,' while 'his citizens hated him and sent a delegation saying we do not want this man to reign over us' -- mirrors a recent, notorious event: Archelaus's voyage to Rome in 4 BCE to be confirmed king, opposed by a Jewish embassy (Josephus, Ant. 17.299-320). The audience would hear the contemporary reference. The settling of accounts uses the 'to everyone who has, more will be given' principle (cf. VI.2-b); Matthew's talents-form drops the throne-claimant frame. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Zechariah 9:9 (the king on a colt); Psalm 118:25-26 (Hosanna, blessed is he who comes); cloaks/branches (2 Kgs 9:13; 1 Macc 13:51)
references.note: The entry stages Zechariah 9:9 -- the king coming 'humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt' -- which Matthew and John quote outright (Zech 9:9 deliberately pairs a peaceable, donkey-riding king against a war-horse). The crowd's 'Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of YHWH' is Psalm 118:25-26, the pilgrim acclamation whose absence was lamented at IX.12-b ('you will not see me until you say...') -- here it is said. The spread cloaks recall royal acclamation (2 Kgs 9:13, Jehu) and the branches the Maccabean rededication processions (1 Macc 13:51; 2 Macc 10:7). Established.

X.2.placement_flag: Grouped under 'anointings' with Luke 7:36-50 (V.6); the Bethany anointing is the burial-anticipating one, days before Passover.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Deuteronomy 15:11 ('the poor will never cease from the land'); anointing/burial; Christos = Anointed
references.note: 'The poor you always have with you' quotes Deuteronomy 15:11 (the same chapter that commands open-handedness, so it is not a counsel of neglect). 'She has anointed my body beforehand for burial' reframes the extravagance as messianic-prophetic: the Anointed (Christos) anointed for death. Distinct from the forgiveness-anointing of V.6. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the fig tree as Israel/temple under judgment (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10,16; Micah 7:1; Joel 1:7)
references.note: Mark INTERCALATES the cursing of the fruitless fig tree around the temple cleansing (X.4): the withered tree interprets the temple's condemnation, and vice versa. The fig tree is the prophets' figure for Israel failing to yield fruit, ripe for judgment (Jer 8:13, 'no figs on the fig tree'; Hos 9:10,16; Mic 7:1; Joel 1:7). The sandwich structure is the message -- the temple, like the tree, is found barren and cursed. Continues IX.10. Established.
scholarship: Telford, The Barren Temple and the Withered Tree

X.4.placement_flag: DISPUTED placement: Synoptics in the final week, John at the start (II.3). The two placements use DIFFERENT citation-bases -- compare here (Isa 56:7 + Jer 7:11) with John's (Ps 69; Zech 14:21) at II.3.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 56:7 ('a house of prayer for all the nations') + Jeremiah 7:11 ('a den of robbers')
references.note: The Synoptic cleansing fuses two prophets: Isaiah 56:7, 'my house shall be called a house of prayer FOR ALL THE NATIONS' (Mark alone keeps the universal 'for all nations,' pointed in the court of the Gentiles), and Jeremiah 7:11, 'a den of robbers (lEstai)' -- Jeremiah's Temple Sermon, where robbery-then-refuge in the temple invites its destruction. The lEstEs note matters: not 'thieves' but brigands/insurgents (glossary). This citation-base is wholly distinct from John's (II.3-a, Ps 69; II.3-b, Zech 14:21), so the disputed double-placement does not double-count. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the counter-question as rabbinic disputation technique
references.note: Jesus parries the authority-question with a counter-question about John's baptism ('from heaven or from men?'), a recognized disputation move that traps the questioners between the crowd and their own skepticism. Form, not citation; light. Possible.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the reversal of insiders/outsiders; 'the way of righteousness' (dikaiosynE)
references.note: The two sons (one says no but goes, one says yes but doesn't) is applied so that toll-collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders, who did not believe John's 'way of righteousness' (dikaiosynE -- glossary). Another insider/outsider reversal; light on direct citation. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 5:1-2 (the Song of the Vineyard)
references.note: The parable opens by quoting the Song of the Vineyard: a man 'planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a wine-press, and built a tower' -- the exact furniture of Isaiah 5:1-2 (LXX). Isaiah's vineyard IS the house of Israel that yields wild grapes and faces ruin; Jesus retains the frame but shifts the indictment from the vineyard to its TENANTS (the leaders). The opening citation tells the hearers the genre and the stakes before the plot turns. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 118:22-23 (the stone the builders rejected)
references.note: Jesus caps the parable with Psalm 118:22-23 -- 'the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone' -- the same psalm that supplied the entry acclamation (X.1-a) and stands behind the passion-prediction's 'rejected' (VIII.2-a). The murdered son and the rejected-then-exalted stone are made to interpret each other. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: non-canonical parallel: Gospel of Thomas 65 (the parable) + 66 (the rejected stone)
references.note: Thomas 65 preserves the tenants WITHOUT the Isaiah-5 allegorical opening and with a sparer plot (and Thomas 66 appends the rejected-stone saying separately). Many read the Thomas form as closer to an original parable about exploitation and reckoning, with the Isaiah-5 framing and the salvation-history allegory (servants = prophets, son = Jesus) as the Synoptic interpretive overlay -- the same kernel/overlay pattern seen with the sower and tares (VI.1-b, VI.6-a). Established.
scholarship: DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on 65-66
Plisch, The Gospel of Thomas, on 65

X.8.placement_flag: Grouped with Luke's great banquet (IX.13) and Thomas 64; Matthew's version adds the king, the burned city, and the wedding garment.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the burning of the city (allusion to the destruction of Jerusalem, 70 CE); cross-ref IX.13-b (the banquet, Thomas 64)
references.note: Matthew's distinctive expansion -- the king sends troops, destroys the murderers, and BURNS THEIR CITY (22:7) -- is widely read as a post-70 allusion to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem read into the parable, a sign of Matthean redaction. The core banquet and its substitution of guests are the Q/Thomas tradition treated at IX.13-b. The wedding-garment appendix (22:11-14) is a separate Matthean addition on readiness. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the coin's image (eikOn) vs. the human as God's image (Genesis 1:27); non-canonical parallel Thomas 100
references.note: 'Whose IMAGE (eikOn) and inscription is this? ... Render to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.' The unspoken second half turns on Genesis 1:27: the denarius bears Caesar's image and returns to Caesar, but the human being bears GOD's image and so belongs wholly to God. The retort both defuses the trap (is the tax lawful?) and quietly relativizes Caesar. Independently attested at Thomas 100, which adds a third clause, 'and give me what is mine.' Probable.
scholarship: DeConick, Original Gospel of Thomas, on 100

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the levirate law (Deuteronomy 25:5-6; cf. Gen 38); Exodus 3:6 ('I am the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob')
references.note: The Sadducees' trick rests on the levirate law (Deut 25:5-6; the seven brothers). Jesus, arguing resurrection from the TORAH alone (the only scripture the Sadducees accepted), cites Exodus 3:6: at the bush God says 'I AM the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' -- present tense -- 'he is not God of the dead but of the living.' A rabbinic-style proof that the patriarchs must live to God. The argument is chosen to meet the Sadducees on their own canon. Established.

X.11.keystone: STRUCTURAL KEYSTONE of the Basileian framework. Matthew 22:40 -- 'on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets' -- is the governing hermeneutical key of Basileianism; the entire canon is read through the double love-command.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Deuteronomy 6:4-5 (the Shema + love God) + Leviticus 19:18 (love neighbor); Matthew 22:40 ('on these two hang all the law and the prophets')
references.note: THE KEYSTONE. Asked for the first commandment, Jesus joins two texts: Deuteronomy 6:4-5, the Shema -- 'Hear, O Israel, YHWH our God, YHWH is one; you shall love YHWH your God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength' -- and Leviticus 19:18, 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself.' Matthew adds the decisive hermeneutical claim: 'on these two commandments HANG all the law and the prophets' (22:40), and Mark's scribe affirms that love outweighs all sacrifice (echoing Hos 6:6; 1 Sam 15:22), to which Jesus replies he is 'not far from the kingdom.' This double love-command is the structuring key of the whole Basileian project: every other text is weighed by its proximity to it. The pairing of Deut 6:5 and Lev 19:18 was itself a live summary move in the period (cf. the lawyer at IX.2-a; Philo; the rabbinic 'love your neighbor' as the great principle). Established.
scholarship: on the double command in Judaism: T. Iss. 5:2; T. Dan 5:3 (with caution)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 110:1 ('YHWH said to my lord, sit at my right hand')
references.note: Jesus poses the riddle from Psalm 110:1 -- the most-cited OT verse in the NT -- 'YHWH (Kyrios) said to my lord (kyriO), sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.' If David calls the Messiah 'my lord,' how is the Messiah merely David's son? The two Kyrios uses must be distinguished per policy (the first = YHWH in the LXX citation; the second = the messianic 'lord'), which is precisely the ambiguity the riddle exploits. Established.
scholarship: Hay, Glory at the Right Hand (Ps 110 in early Christianity)

X.13.canon_title: Woes on the scribes and Pharisees

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Micah 6:8 (justice, mercy, and faithfulness -- 'the weightier matters of the law')
references.note: The woe against tithing 'mint, dill, and cumin' while neglecting 'justice, mercy, and faithfulness -- the weightier matters of the law' restates Micah 6:8 ('to do justice, love mercy, walk humbly'). The phylacteries and fringes of 23:5 reference Deut 6:8 and Num 15:38-39 worn for show. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Genesis 4:8 (the blood of Abel) to 2 Chronicles 24:20-22 (the blood of Zechariah)
references.note: 'From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar' spans the murdered righteous from the FIRST book of the Hebrew Bible (Gen 4:8) to the LAST in the Jewish ordering (2 Chronicles, where the priest Zechariah is stoned in the temple court, 24:20-22). A whole-canon inclusio of prophetic blood -- 'Genesis to Chronicles' rather than 'Genesis to Malachi.' Cross-ref IX.5-a. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the reversal of true vs. ostentatious giving; juxtaposed with 'devouring widows' houses' (12:40)
references.note: The widow's two copper coins -- 'all she had to live on' -- outweigh the rich gifts by the measure of cost, a great-reversal valuation. Placed immediately after the charge that the scribes 'devour widows' houses' (12:40), it may read as lament as much as praise (the piety system that consumes the poor widow's last coin), a tension worth flagging rather than flattening. Possible.
scholarship: Marcus, AYB Mark, on 12:41-44 (the lament reading)

X.15.canon_title: Greeks seek Jesus; the voice from heaven

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the grain of wheat dying to bear fruit; the voice from heaven (bat qol, cf. I.2, VIII.3); 'lifted up' (cf. II.4-b)
references.note: 'Unless a grain of wheat falls and dies, it remains alone' makes the agricultural commonplace a figure of redemptive death. The heavenly voice (12:28) is the third Johannine/Synoptic bat qol after the baptism (I.2-a) and transfiguration (VIII.3-a). 'When I am lifted up' continues the hypsoO crucifixion-exaltation pun of II.4-b. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 53:1 ('who has believed our report?') + Isaiah 6:10 (the blinded eyes)
references.note: John explains the people's unbelief with two Isaiah citations: 53:1, 'Lord, who has believed our message?' (the Servant Song's opening), and 6:10, the blinding and hardening (the same parable-purpose text as VI.1-a). John even says Isaiah 'saw his glory and spoke of him' (12:41). The Servant rejection and the judicial hardening together account for the failure of faith. Established.
scholarship: Menken, OT Quotations in the Fourth Gospel

X.16.canon_title: The Olivet discourse (the end of the age)
X.16.placement_flag: 1 Thess 4:15-17 ('a word of the Lord' on the coming) grouped here; whether it reports a dominical saying or a later prophetic word is debated -- flagged, not resolved.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11 (the abomination of desolation); cosmic signs (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10,31; Ezek 32:7)
references.note: The discourse is woven from Daniel and the prophets. 'The abomination of desolation' (with Mark's aside 'let the reader understand') is Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11 -- originally Antiochus's altar, reapplied to a coming desecration. The darkened sun and moon and falling stars splice Isaiah 13:10, 34:4, Joel 2:10,31, and Ezekiel 32:7 -- the stock cosmic-collapse imagery of the Day of the LORD. Established.
scholarship: Beasley-Murray, Jesus and the Last Days

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:13-14 (the son of man coming on the clouds); the gathering of the elect (Zech 2:6; Deut 30:4)
references.note: 'They will see the son of humanity coming in clouds with great power and glory' quotes Daniel 7:13-14, the one like a son of man given dominion -- the climactic use of the title-text footnoted from its first occurrence (per the divine-names policy on huios tou anthrOpou). The angels 'gather the elect from the four winds' draws on the regathering promises (Zech 2:6; Deut 30:4). The grouped 1 Thess 4:15-17 ('the Lord himself will descend... and the dead will rise') gives an early-50s 'word of the Lord' on the same coming, whose dominical status is flagged as debated. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the delayed bridegroom (cf. II.5-a, III.7-a); eschatological watchfulness; the shut door
references.note: The wise and foolish bridesmaids awaiting the delayed bridegroom extend the bridegroom-motif (the covenant bridegroom, II.5-a; the wedding-guests, III.7-a) into an allegory of readiness for the delayed parousia. 'I do not know you' and the shut door echo the narrow-door warning (IX.12-a). Probable.

X.18.placement_flag: Grouped with Luke's pounds (IX.33), which carries the Archelaus throne-claimant frame; Matthew's talents-form is treated there.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-ref: 'to everyone who has, more will be given' (VI.2-b); the entrusted-money reckoning (IX.33)
references.note: The talents reprise the entrusted-money reckoning of Luke's pounds (IX.33) and close on 'to everyone who has, more will be given' (cf. VI.2-b, Thomas 41). Cross-reference. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:13-14 (the son of man enthroned in glory); Ezekiel 34:17 (the shepherd judging between sheep and goats); the nations gathered (Joel 3:2,12)
references.note: The judgment scene seats 'the son of humanity on his glorious throne' (Daniel 7:13-14) and has him 'separate the sheep from the goats AS A SHEPHERD does' -- Ezekiel 34:17, where God-the-shepherd 'judges between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats.' The nations are gathered for judgment as in Joel 3:2,12. The criterion -- treatment of the hungry, naked, sick, imprisoned 'least of these,' identified with the king himself -- enacts the love-of-neighbor keystone (X.11) as the measure of judgment. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Zechariah 11:12-13 (the thirty pieces of silver, the potter); cf. Exodus 21:32 (the price of a slave); Gen 37:28 (Joseph sold)
references.note: Matthew alone fixes Judas's price at 'thirty pieces of silver,' the contemptuous wage weighed out in Zechariah 11:12-13 and cast to the potter -- which Matthew will later quote outright at the field of blood (27:9-10, there mis-attributed to Jeremiah). Thirty shekels is also the compensation for a gored slave (Exod 21:32), and the betrayal-by-sale recalls Joseph (Gen 37:28). Mark and Luke do not name the sum. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Passover (Exodus 12); the Synoptic/Johannine dating crux
references.note: The meal is set within Passover (Exod 12, the lamb and unleavened bread). The famous chronological crux belongs here: the Synoptics make the Supper itself the Passover meal (the lamb slain that afternoon), while John dates the crucifixion to Passover eve (Jesus dying as the lambs are killed, John 19:14) -- a difference of one day that serves John's lamb-of-God typology (II.1-a). Flagged as the structural background; the divergence is theological, not merely calendrical. Established.
scholarship: Jeremias, The Eucharistic Words of Jesus (the dating debate)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 41:9 ('the one who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me')
references.note: Jesus performs the slave's task -- washing the disciples' feet -- as the enacted lesson of humble service, then quotes Psalm 41:9 of the betrayer: 'the one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me.' The psalm is the lament of one betrayed by an intimate table-companion, which is exactly Judas's position at the meal; sharing the table makes the betrayal a covenant-breach. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 41:9 (the table-companion betrayer, cf. XI.2-a); the 'as it is written' passion necessity (Isa 53; Ps 22)
references.note: 'One of you will betray me, one who is dipping bread with me in the dish' alludes to Psalm 41:9 (explicitly quoted in John, XI.2-a). Jesus adds the scriptural-necessity formula: 'the son of humanity goes AS IT IS WRITTEN of him' -- the passion is read as fulfilling Scripture (the suffering Servant of Isa 53, the righteous sufferer of Ps 22) -- 'but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed.' Necessity and culpability held together. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Exodus 24:8 (the blood of the covenant) + Jeremiah 31:31 (the new covenant) + Zechariah 9:11; 'for many' = Isaiah 53:11-12
references.note: 'This is my blood of the COVENANT, poured out for many' fuses Exodus 24:8 -- Moses dashing the covenant-blood on the people, 'the blood of the covenant' -- with the promise of a NEW covenant in Jeremiah 31:31 (which Luke and Paul make explicit: 'the new covenant in my blood'), and the covenant-blood of release in Zechariah 9:11. 'Poured out FOR MANY' echoes Isaiah 53:11-12, the Servant who bore the sin of the many -- binding the cup to the ransom saying of IX.30-b. The Passover frame (Exod 12) supplies the setting. Established.
scholarship: Jeremias, The Eucharistic Words of Jesus

references.speaker: other
references.source: inner-canon: Paul's transmitted tradition ('I received... I handed on'), the earliest written account of the Supper
references.note: Paul's account (c. 54, before any Gospel) is the EARLIEST written report of the institution, framed as fixed tradition -- 'I RECEIVED from the Lord what I also HANDED ON to you' (the technical paradosis language) -- 'that the Lord Jesus, on the night he was handed over...'. It transmits the bread, the cup as 'the new covenant in my blood,' and the 'do this in remembrance,' independently confirming the words a generation before Mark. A capstone example of the canon's logic for admitting Paul as a tradent of dominical material (cf. IV.4-b, VII.5-a). Established.
scholarship: Hengel and Schwemer, on the pre-Pauline tradition

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:9-10,22 (thrones set, judgment given to the holy ones); the twelve-tribe restoration (cf. III.11-a)
references.note: Against the dispute over greatness -- answered by the servant-leadership reversal (cf. IX.30) -- Jesus promises the Twelve that they 'will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.' The enthroned judges draw on Daniel 7:9-10,22, where thrones are set and judgment is given to the holy ones of the Most High, and the number reasserts the restoration of the twelve tribes (III.11-a). Established.
scholarship: Dan 7:9-10,22; Davies-Allison, ICC Matthew III, on 19:28

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Zechariah 13:7 ('strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered')
references.note: 'You will all fall away, for it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered' quotes Zechariah 13:7 -- the smitten shepherd of the LORD whose striking scatters the flock. The citation casts the disciples' imminent desertion as scripturally foreseen, and joins the shepherd-Christology already gathered (Ezek 34; Good Shepherd, IX.23-a). The promise 'after I am raised I will go before you to Galilee' immediately follows. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Israel as the vine: Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7; 27:2-3; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; 17; 19
references.note: 'I am the TRUE vine' rewrites the OT figure of Israel as God's vine/vineyard -- the vine brought out of Egypt (Ps 80:8-16), the vineyard that yielded wild grapes (Isa 5:1-7; 27:2-3), the 'choice vine' turned degenerate (Jer 2:21; Ezek 15,17,19). Where Israel-the-vine failed to bear fruit, Jesus is the TRUE vine and the disciples its branches: another Johannine replacement (cf. the temple, II.3; the manna, VII.11) in which Jesus takes up and fulfills an institution of Israel. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the ParaklEtos (Advocate/Comforter); 'the spirit of truth' (cf. Qumran, 1QS 3:18-4:26)
references.note: The promised ParaklEtos -- Advocate, Helper, Comforter (glossary term, left transliterated on first occurrence) -- is named the 'Spirit of truth.' The forensic 'advocate/intercessor' role has Jewish-angelological background (the intercessory angel/figure), and the 'spirit of truth' set against the world's deceiving spirit closely parallels the Two-Spirits doctrine at Qumran (1QS 3:18-4:26, the Spirit of truth vs. the spirit of deceit). The exact lexical range of paraklEtos is the standing question (advocate / comforter / helper). Probable for the Qumran resonance; established that the term needs the glossary treatment.
scholarship: Brown, AYB John, on the Paraclete (Appendix V)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the revealed divine NAME (Exod 3:14-15; Ezek 36:23); aiOnios ('of-the-age'); 'son of perdition... that scripture be fulfilled' (Ps 41:9; Ps 109:8)
references.note: The consecration prayer turns on the NAME: 'I have manifested your name' / 'I kept them in your name which you gave me' (17:6,12), the revealed divine name of Exodus 3 and the sanctified name of Ezekiel 36:23 (cf. the Lord's Prayer, IV.6-a). 'This is aiOnios life -- to know you' should be read 'life of-the-age' rather than 'eternal life' (glossary: aiOn/aiOnios). The loss of 'the son of perdition, that the scripture might be fulfilled' (17:12) points back to the betrayer-psalm (Ps 41:9; cf. Ps 109:8, the office given to another). Probable.
scholarship: Exod 3:14-15; Ezek 36:23; on aiOnios: BDAG / glossary

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 42:5,11; 43:5 ('why are you cast down, O my soul'); the cup of wrath (Isa 51:17; Jer 25:15; cf. IX.30-a); Abba
references.note: 'My soul is very sorrowful, even to death' echoes the refrain of the lament psalms, 'why are you cast down, O my soul' (Ps 42:5,11; 43:5). The prayer to 'remove this CUP' invokes the cup of God's wrath/judgment (Isa 51:17; Jer 25:15; cf. IX.30-a), now drained in person. 'ABBA, Father' preserves the Aramaic address (transliterated per the divine-names policy on Abba), and 'the spirit is willing but the FLESH (sarx) is weak' carries the glossary term. The fully human dread is the divergence from any serene-martyr convention. Established.
scholarship: Ps 42-43; on Abba: Jeremias, The Prayers of Jesus

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: lEstEs ('bandit/insurgent', glossary); 'let the scriptures be fulfilled'; the fleeing naked youth (Amos 2:16)
references.note: 'Have you come out as against a BANDIT (lEstEs) with swords and clubs?' uses the loaded term for an insurgent/brigand (glossary; the same word for the two crucified beside him, XII.7), framing the arrest as treating Jesus like a rebel. 'Let the scriptures be fulfilled' states the passion-necessity without a single citation. The young man who flees naked (Mark only) may glance at Amos 2:16, 'the stout of heart shall flee naked in that day.' Matthew's 'all who take the sword perish by the sword' (26:52) is proverbial. Probable.

XII.3.canon_title: Before Annas and Caiaphas; the Sanhedrin

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:13 (the son of man on the clouds) + Psalm 110:1 (seated at the right hand)
references.note: Asked if he is the Anointed, the son of the Blessed, Jesus answers with the two great enthronement texts FUSED: 'you will see the son of humanity SEATED AT THE RIGHT HAND of Power (Psalm 110:1) and COMING WITH THE CLOUDS of heaven (Daniel 7:13).' This single sentence joins the canon's two most-used messianic prooftexts (Ps 110, the David's-Lord riddle of X.12; Dan 7, the Olivet coming of X.16-b) and triggers the blasphemy verdict. The climactic christological claim of the Synoptic passion. Established.
scholarship: Bock, Blasphemy and Exaltation in Judaism

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the false witnesses (Psalm 27:12; 35:11); the silent accused (Isaiah 53:7); the temple-saying (cf. II.3-c)
references.note: 'Many bore FALSE WITNESS against him' and 'their testimony did not agree' colors the trial with the lament-psalms' false witnesses (Ps 27:12; 35:11). Jesus's silence -- 'he was silent and answered nothing' (14:61) -- evokes the Servant who 'opened not his mouth' (Isa 53:7). The garbled temple-destruction charge (14:58, 'I will destroy this temple made with hands') is the misremembered saying of II.3-c. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: fulfillment of the denial prediction (cross-ref XI.6); the cock-crow
