references.note: The triple denial and the cock-crow fulfill Jesus's prediction at XI.6 (which itself quoted Zech 13:7 on the scattered sheep). The scene is narrative fulfillment rather than fresh OT citation -- logged as the closing of that prediction. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Zechariah 11:12-13 (thirty pieces, the potter) blended with Jeremiah (18-19; 32:6-9) -- mis-attributed by Matthew to 'Jeremiah'
references.note: ANOTHER mis-attribution seam. Matthew quotes the thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter 'in the house of the LORD' -- which is ZECHARIAH 11:12-13 (cf. X.20) -- but credits it to 'the prophet JEREMIAH' (27:9), apparently blending in Jeremiah's potter and field-purchase (Jer 18-19; 32:6-9). This is the New Testament's most discussed citation-error, exactly parallel to Mark's Malachi-as-Isaiah slip (I.1-a): an evangelist naming the wrong prophet for a composite citation. A direct datapoint for the apparatus's recurring seam. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 53:7 (silent before the shearers)
references.note: Jesus's refusal to answer Pilate's charges, 'so that Pilate was amazed,' continues the Servant's silence of Isaiah 53:7 (the lamb dumb before its shearers; cf. XII.3-b). The silence before two tribunals frames Jesus as the uncomplaining Servant. Probable.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Psalm 2:1-2 (the kings and rulers gather against the LORD's anointed)
references.note: Luke's distinctive Herod scene -- Herod and Pilate, formerly enemies, become friends that day over Jesus -- is read by Luke himself through Psalm 2:1-2: the early church cites this very episode as the fulfillment of 'the kings of the earth set themselves... against the LORD and his Anointed' (Acts 4:25-27 names Herod and Pilate). The gathered rulers against the Anointed. Probable; explicit in Acts.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Psalm 22:18 (dividing garments, casting lots)
references.note: 'They divided his garments, casting lots for them' is Psalm 22:18, 'they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots' -- which John quotes outright as fulfillment (19:24). Psalm 22, the lament of the righteous sufferer, supplies the script for the entire crucifixion scene (continued at XII.7-b and the death-cry XII.8-a). Established.
scholarship: Brown, The Death of the Messiah (Ps 22 in the passion)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Psalm 22:7-8 (mockers wag their heads; 'he trusts in God, let God deliver him'); the two lEstai = Isaiah 53:12 ('numbered with transgressors')
references.note: The mockery is Psalm 22:7-8 verbatim in shape: 'those who passed by derided him, WAGGING THEIR HEADS' (Ps 22:7), and Matthew's 'he trusts in God, let God deliver him now' (27:43) is Psalm 22:8. The two BANDITS (lEstai) crucified with him fulfill Isaiah 53:12, 'he was numbered with the transgressors' (cited explicitly in some Mark MSS at 15:28). Luke's penitent thief and 'today in paradise' is special material. Established.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 22:1 ('my God, my God, why have you forsaken me')
references.note: The death-cry is Psalm 22:1, given in Aramaic ('Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani') -- closer to the Targum than the Hebrew 'Eli' -- which is what lets bystanders mishear it as a call to Eli-jah. Opening the very psalm whose details have scripted the scene (garments, mockery), the cry is heard by many as dereliction and by the tradition as the first line of a psalm that ends in vindication. The single most weighed verse of the passion. Established.
scholarship: Brown, The Death of the Messiah

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: noon darkness (Amos 8:9); the torn sanctuary veil (Exod 26:31-34; Lev 16:2); Greco-Roman death-portent convention; imperial acclamation inverted
references.note: The death-portents -- the apparatus's inaugural worked example. Darkness over the land at noon alludes to Amos 8:9 ('I will make the sun go down at noon... mourning as for an only son') AND deploys the Greco-Roman convention of cosmic disturbance at a great man's death -- but inverted, paired with dereliction rather than apotheosis. The torn sanctuary veil (Exod 26:31-34; Lev 16:2) is rent with the same violent verb (schizO) as the heavens at the baptism (I.2-a), bracketing the Gospel. The centurion's 'truly this man was God's son' inverts the imperial acclamation of Caesar as divi filius. (Pure text-critical items here -- e.g. Luke 23:34a 'Father forgive them' -- belong to the text-critical layer; note only that its content echoes Isa 53:12, the Servant interceding for transgressors.) Established.
scholarship: on the portent convention: Collins ad loc.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Psalm 31:5 ('into your hands I commit my spirit')
references.note: Luke replaces the cry of dereliction with a different psalm: 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit' is Psalm 31:5, a prayer of trustful surrender (Luke adds 'Father'). Each evangelist gives Jesus a final psalm-word -- Mark/Matthew the forsaken-cry of Ps 22:1, Luke the trust of Ps 31:5, John 'it is finished' -- a redactional divergence in the dying words themselves. Established.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Psalm 69:21 (vinegar for thirst); the unbroken bones (Exod 12:46; Num 9:12; Ps 34:20); Zechariah 12:10 (the pierced one)
references.note: John reads the death through three texts he names as fulfilled. 'I thirst,' answered with sour wine, completes Psalm 69:21 ('for my thirst they gave me vinegar'; cf. the gall at XII.7 / Mark 15:36). 'Not one of his bones shall be broken' (19:36) cites the Passover-lamb rule (Exod 12:46; Num 9:12) and Psalm 34:20 -- making the crucified the true Passover lamb (the lamb-of-God of II.1-a, and John's Passover-eve dating, XI.1-a). 'They will look on the one they have pierced' (19:37) is Zechariah 12:10. Established.

XII.9.placement_flag: The Gospel of Peter (Akhmim fragment) is admitted for its passion/burial material ONLY; its talking cross, giant Jesus, and resurrection-witnessing soldiers are excluded as later embellishment.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: Isaiah 53:9 ('with the rich in his death'); non-canonical witness: Gospel of Peter (burial)
references.note: Joseph of Arimathea -- whom Matthew calls 'a RICH man' (27:57) -- lays Jesus in his own new rock tomb, fulfilling Isaiah 53:9, 'they made his grave with the wicked and with a RICH man in his death.' The Gospel of Peter preserves an independent passion/burial narrative admitted here for that material only; its embellishments (the talking cross, the giant Jesus, the soldiers who witness the resurrection) are excluded as secondary legend -- a clean instance of the canon's source-triage applied to a non-canonical text. Probable for Isa 53:9; the Gospel of Peter logged as a controlled witness.
scholarship: Brown, The Death of the Messiah, on the burial
Foster, The Gospel of Peter (commentary and triage)

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: 'on the third day' (Hosea 6:2; cf. the sign of Jonah, V.10); women as first witnesses
references.note: The announcement 'he has been raised, he is not here' falls on the third day, the interval already loaded by Hosea 6:2 ('on the third day he will raise us up') and the sign of Jonah (V.10). The witnesses are WOMEN -- a detail that runs against the conventions of credible testimony in the period, often weighed as a mark of authenticity rather than design. Mark's abrupt close at 16:8 ('they were afraid') is the original ending; the longer ending (16:9-20) is text-critically secondary and belongs to that layer. Probable.
scholarship: Metzger, Textual Commentary, on the endings of Mark

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: the garden setting and the beloved sought-and-found (Song of Songs 3:1-4); Mary as first witness
references.note: Mary weeping in the GARDEN, seeking the one she loves and at last finding him, faintly recalls the Song of Songs -- 'I sought him whom my soul loves... I found him' (Song 3:1-4) -- a new-creation garden answering Eden (the garden tomb, 19:41). Mary, sent to announce the rising, becomes the first witness and herald (the later tradition's 'apostle to the apostles'). The Song echo is suggestive, not marked; possible.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: apologetic counter to the stolen-body polemic
references.note: Matthew's notice that the guards were bribed to say 'his disciples stole him,' a story told 'among the Jews to this day,' is an apologetic answer to a circulating anti-resurrection polemic (later echoed in Justin and the Toledot Yeshu tradition). Historical-cultural/polemical, not OT citation. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the whole of Scripture read christologically: 'Moses and all the prophets' (24:27); 'the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms' (24:44) -- the tripartite Hebrew canon
references.note: THE apparatus's own charter, placed on the lips of the risen Jesus. 'Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself' (24:27), and later, 'everything written about me in the LAW OF MOSES, THE PROPHETS, AND THE PSALMS must be fulfilled' (24:44) -- naming the tripartite Hebrew canon (Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim). 'Was it not NECESSARY that the Anointed should suffer these things and enter his glory?' supplies the hermeneutic that drives the whole passion-citation network of Part XII: the suffering-then-vindication read out of all Scripture. The recognition 'in the breaking of bread' ties it to the Supper (XI.4). This is the canon's own theory of how Jesus reads -- and is read in -- the Scriptures. Established.
scholarship: on Luke's use of Scripture: Bock, Proclamation from Prophecy and Pattern

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Genesis 2:7 (the breath of life); Ezekiel 37:9-10 (breath into the slain); the opening of minds to Scripture (cf. XIII.4)
references.note: John's 'he BREATHED on them and said, receive the Holy Spirit' (20:22) deliberately uses the verb of Genesis 2:7, where God breathes the breath of life into the human -- a new creation -- with overtones of Ezekiel 37:9-10, the breath entering the slain to make them live. Luke's parallel has Jesus 'open their minds to understand the scriptures' (24:45), continuing the Emmaus hermeneutic (XIII.4). The eating of fish (24:42-43) is an anti-docetic proof of bodily resurrection. Probable.

references.speaker: other
references.source: 'my Lord and my God' (kyrios + theos); cf. Ps 35:23; the divine-titles of the Fourth Gospel's frame (John 1:1)
references.note: Thomas's confession 'my Lord and my GOD' (ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou) is the climactic christological acclamation of the Gospel, echoing the worshipper's address to God in the Psalms ('my God and my Lord,' Ps 35:23) and closing the inclusio with the prologue's 'the Word was God' (John 1:1). 'Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe' turns to later readers. The Kyrios/Theos pairing is the high-water mark for the divine-names policy. Probable.

XIII.7.canon_title: By the Sea of Tiberias; Peter restored

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: the shepherd commission ('feed/tend my sheep'); Ezekiel 34 / the Good Shepherd (cf. IX.23-a); agapaO/phileO (glossary: agapE/philia)
references.note: Peter's threefold 'do you love me?' undoes the threefold denial (XII.4), and the commission 'feed my lambs / tend my sheep / feed my sheep' hands on the shepherd's office grounded in Ezekiel 34 and the Good Shepherd discourse (IX.23-a). The dialogue alternates agapaO and phileO for 'love' -- the agapE/philia distinction flagged in the glossary -- though whether the variation is meaningful or stylistic is debated and should not be over-pressed. The miraculous catch (153 fish) recalls the call (Luke 5). Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Daniel 7:14 (all authority/dominion over the nations given to the son of man); 'I am with you' (Exod 3:12; Hag 1:13) closing the Immanuel inclusio (Matt 1:23)
references.note: 'ALL AUTHORITY in heaven and on earth has been given to me' is the enthronement of Daniel 7:14, where 'dominion and glory and kingship' are given to the one like a son of man, 'that all peoples should serve him' -- the risen Jesus now receives the universal authority the trial-saying foretold (XII.3-a). 'Make disciples of ALL NATIONS' realizes the Gentile ingathering threaded through the canon (the 70, V/VII; the banquet, IX.13). 'I am WITH YOU always' (the divine assurance, Exod 3:12; Hag 1:13) closes Matthew's inclusio with 'Immanuel, God with us' (1:23). Established.
scholarship: on the inclusio: Kupp, Matthew's Emmanuel

parallels: Gospel of the Hebrews (the appearance to James, per Jerome)

references.speaker: other
references.source: the pre-Pauline creed: 'died for our sins ACCORDING TO THE SCRIPTURES' (Isaiah 53) and 'raised on the third day ACCORDING TO THE SCRIPTURES' (Hosea 6:2; Ps 16:10; cf. Jonah)
references.note: The capstone of the canon's intertextual logic AND of its Paul-as-tradent thread. Paul transmits a formula he 'RECEIVED' and 'HANDED ON' (the paradosis language of XI.4-b), almost universally dated to within a few years of the crucifixion -- the earliest datable resurrection tradition. Its twin refrain, 'according to the scriptures,' is the canon's own claim about itself: that Christ 'died for our sins' fulfills Isaiah 53, and 'was raised on the third day' fulfills Hosea 6:2 / Psalm 16:10 (and the Jonah sign, V.10). The appearance LIST -- Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles -- is the bedrock witness-tradition; the appearance to James is independently preserved in the Gospel of the Hebrews (cited by Jerome), a controlled non-canonical witness. Three of the canon's four Paul-as-reporter nodes (IV.4-b, VII.5-a, XI.4-b) culminate here. Established.
scholarship: Hengel and Schwemer; on the Gospel of the Hebrews: Jerome, De viris illustribus 2

XIII.10.placement_flag: CANON TERMINUS. The ascension (Mark 16:19; Luke 24:50-53; Acts 1:9-11) marks Jesus leaving earthly presence and is the closing boundary of the canon under criterion 3 (pre-departure material only).

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: Isaiah 49:6 ('to the ends of the earth'); the forty days (cf. the wilderness forty, I.3-a)
references.note: The final words before the ascension -- 'you will be my witnesses... to the END OF THE EARTH' -- echo Isaiah 49:6, the Servant given 'as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' (Luke makes the citation explicit later at Acts 13:47). The forty days of resurrection teaching about 'the kingdom of God' round off the forty-day wilderness testing that opened the ministry (I.3-a), bracketing the whole canon between two forties. The ascension that follows is the terminus. Established -- and a fitting close: the canon ends pointing outward to all nations, the keystone's love-of-neighbor (X.11) sent to the ends of the earth.
scholarship: on Acts 1:8 and Isa 49:6: Pao, Acts and the Isaianic New Exodus

references.speaker: other
references.source: the 'pangs of death' (Psalm 18:4-5; 116:3 LXX, Odines thanatou); the 'definite plan' = scriptural necessity
references.note: The compressed kerygma -- Jesus 'delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,' whom God raised 'loosing the PANGS of death, because it was not possible for him to be held' -- echoes the Psalms' Odines thanatou, the 'birth-pangs/cords of death' (Ps 18:4-5; 116:3 LXX, where the Greek renders the Hebrew 'cords' as 'birth-pangs'). The fuller Pentecost speech goes on to quote Joel 2, Psalm 16:8-11, and Psalm 110:1, but this canon-slice is the summary; the 'definite plan' asserts the passion's scriptural necessity without naming a text. Probable.

A.2.canon_title: Peter in the house of Cornelius (kerygma)

references.speaker: other
references.source: Isaiah 52:7 / Nahum 1:15 (good news of peace); Isaiah 61:1 (anointed with the Spirit, cf. II.9-a); Deuteronomy 21:22-23 ('hanged on a tree'); Hosea 6:2 (third day)
references.note: A whole ministry summarized through the prophets. 'Preaching GOOD NEWS of PEACE through Jesus Christ' echoes Isaiah 52:7 / Nahum 1:15, the herald who publishes peace; 'God ANOINTED Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power' is Isaiah 61:1 (the Anointed of Nazareth, cf. II.9-a) and Isaiah 42:1; 'they killed him by HANGING him on a TREE' invokes Deuteronomy 21:22-23, the curse of the one hung on a tree that the early church used to interpret crucifixion (cf. Gal 3:13); 'God raised him on the THIRD DAY' draws on Hosea 6:2 (cf. XIII.9); and 'to him all the PROPHETS bear witness' states the fulfillment-claim. The kerygma is the Gospel narrative compressed into its prooftexts. Established.
scholarship: on the kerygma: Dodd, The Apostolic Preaching and Its Developments

references.speaker: other
references.source: 2 Samuel 7:12 / Psalm 132:11 (the Davidic-dynasty promise of a Savior); the prophets 'read every Sabbath' fulfilled (cf. XIII.4); Deuteronomy 21:23 ('took him down from the tree')
references.note: Paul's summary roots Jesus in the Davidic promise: 'of this man's offspring God brought to Israel a SAVIOR, Jesus, as he PROMISED' -- 2 Samuel 7:12 / Psalm 132:11, the oath to set David's offspring on the throne. The leaders, 'because they did not recognize him nor the UTTERANCES OF THE PROPHETS read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him' (13:27) -- the same all-Scripture-fulfilled hermeneutic as Emmaus (XIII.4). 'They took him down from the TREE' repeats the Deut 21:23 motif (A.2-a). The fuller speech (13:33-35) goes on to quote Ps 2:7, Isa 55:3, Ps 16:10; this slice carries the Davidic-promise frame. Established.

B.1.canon_title: 'More blessed to give than to receive' (agraphon)

references.speaker: other
references.source: an AGRAPHON: a saying of Jesus found in no Gospel; Greco-Roman benefaction maxims (Thucydides 2.97; Aristotle, NE 4.1)
references.note: The canon's clearest free-floating dominical saying. Paul, in his Miletus farewell, urges support of the weak, 'REMEMBERING THE WORDS OF THE LORD JESUS, that he himself said: it is more blessed to GIVE than to RECEIVE' -- a saying preserved in no Gospel (the definition of an agraphon). The sentiment has Greco-Roman maxim parallels on the honor of the giver over the receiver (Thucydides 2.97.4; Aristotle), but it is here transmitted explicitly as a remembered word of Jesus -- early, attributed, and unanchored to any scene. A model case for the canon's inclusion of reliably-attested dominical material outside the four Gospels. Established as an agraphon.
scholarship: Jeremias, Unknown Sayings of Jesus (on the agrapha)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: inner vs. outer purity (cf. Mark 7, VII.12; Matt 23 whitewashed tombs, X.13-b); temple immersion-purity practice
references.note: The fragment stages a temple confrontation: a chief-priest Pharisee (named Levi) challenges Jesus for entering the holy place without the prescribed immersion. Jesus answers with the inner/outer-purity polemic familiar from Mark 7 (VII.12) and the whitewashed-tombs woe (X.13-b): the opponents wash in 'poured-out waters' yet are inwardly defiled, while he and his are washed in 'living water from heaven.' The fragment's temple topography (a 'pool of David,' the immersion of priests) is debated -- some judge it authentic local detail, others a later composition with garbled geography -- so the witness is logged at POSSIBLE, with the authenticity question flagged rather than resolved.
scholarship: Kruger, The Gospel of the Savior / on P.Oxy 840

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-refs: the physician/meal-controversy (III.6-c); 'whoever is not against you is for you' (VIII.8, Mark 9:40); 'pray for your enemies' (IV.3-f, Matt 5:44)
references.note: The fragment preserves several sayings independently of the canonical wording. Besides the meal-controversy with its added 'priests' (already at III.6-c), it carries 'he who is not against you is for you' (cf. the strange exorcist, VIII.8 / Mark 9:40) and an exhortation to 'pray for your enemies' (cf. the love-enemy antithesis, IV.3-f / Matt 5:44). A fragmentary, independent witness to sayings otherwise in the Synoptic stream. Probable.

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-refs: the rich-fool ending (IX.7-a); 'add a cubit' (IV.7-c); 'fast from the kosmos / keep the Sabbath' = Thomas 27
references.note: A recently published papyrus carrying a cluster of sayings that overlap Q and Thomas: the ending of the rich fool (cf. IX.7-a), the 'which of you can add a cubit' worry-saying (cf. IV.7-c), and 'if you do not fast from the WORLD (kosmos)... if you do not keep the SABBATH as a Sabbath, you will not see the Father' -- which is Thomas 27. FRESHNESS FLAG (as at IV.7-c): the editio princeps is recent and its readings and tradition-relationships are still under scholarly assessment, so the whole fragment is held at possible pending verification. A potential new witness to the sayings tradition.
scholarship: P.Oxy 5575 (Oxyrhynchus Papyri vol. 87) -- verify readings at build time

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: John 5:39,45 (searching the scriptures that witness to me); a leper-cleansing (cf. III.4); Isaiah 29:13 in the tribute question (the SAME text as Mark 7:6, VII.12-a)
references.note: One of the earliest gospel fragments, and striking because it MIXES Johannine and Synoptic material. It has Jesus tell the authorities, 'you SEARCH THE SCRIPTURES... it is they that bear witness to me' and 'do not think I came to accuse you to the Father' -- John 5:39,45 nearly verbatim. It then narrates a LEPER-cleansing (the leper says he caught it 'eating with lepers'; cf. III.4), and a TRIBUTE question -- 'is it lawful to pay kings what belongs to their rule?' -- which Jesus rebuffs by quoting ISAIAH 29:13, 'this people honors me with their lips' (the very text of Mark 7:6, VII.12-a). A fragmentary riverside nature-miracle closes it. Whether Egerton is pre-Synoptic, independent, or a harmonizing pastiche of John + the Synoptics is debated; logged as a probable witness with that question flagged.
scholarship: Kruger / Lührmann, Fragmente apokryph gewordener Evangelien

B.6.placement_flag: Borderline status: liturgical prayers, not a saying or deed of Jesus; admitted as early dominical-community material with that flag.

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: 'the holy VINE of David' (Ps 80; the true vine, XI.7-a); the bread 'scattered on the mountains and gathered into one' (eschatological ingathering)
references.note: The earliest eucharistic prayers (c. 100) give thanks 'for the holy VINE of David your servant' (Did 9:2) -- joining the Davidic-vine of Psalm 80 to the True-Vine Christology of XI.7-a -- and pray that as the broken bread 'was scattered over the mountains and gathered into one, so let the church be gathered from the ends of the earth into your kingdom' (9:4), the eschatological ingathering. Liturgical reception rather than dominical saying (hence the borderline flag), but it shows the vine and ingathering motifs already shaping worship. Probable.

B.7.canon_title: Thomas sayings without a narrative anchor (41, 86, 113)

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: cross-refs: Logion 41 ('whoever has, more given', VI.2-b); Logion 86 (foxes/holes = Matt 8:20 // Luke 9:58, cf. IX.1); Logion 113 (kingdom spread out, IX.18-a)
references.note: The Thomas logia that have no narrative home in the harmony are gathered here. Logion 41, 'whoever has, to him will be given' (the measure-reciprocity of VI.2-b). Logion 86, 'the foxes have their holes and the birds their nests, but the son of man has nowhere to lay his head' -- the homelessness saying of Matt 8:20 // Luke 9:58 (the would-be follower of IX.1). Logion 113, 'the kingdom is spread out upon the earth and people do not see it' (already at IX.18-a). All multiply attested with the Synoptics. Established.
scholarship: DeConick, The Original Gospel of Thomas, on 41, 86, 113

references.speaker: Jesus
references.source: an AGRAPHON in the Western text; coheres with the Sabbath-controversy (Mark 2:23-28, III.8; 'Sabbath for man', III.8-c)
references.note: Codex Bezae inserts after Luke 6:4 an otherwise-unknown scene: 'On the same day, seeing someone working on the Sabbath, he said to him: Man, if you KNOW what you are doing, you are BLESSED; but if you do not know, you are ACCURSED and a transgressor of the law.' Jeremias's single most-cited candidate for an authentic agraphon -- Palestinian in flavor, paradoxical in the manner of the genuine Sabbath sayings, and cohering with Mark 2:23-28 (III.8) and 'the Sabbath was made for man' (III.8-c). Its knowledge-as-the-criterion logic is distinctive. Authenticity is argued (Jeremias) and contested; logged at possible.
scholarship: Jeremias, Unknown Sayings of Jesus, on the Bezan agraphon

references.speaker: narrator
references.source: apostolic fathers quoting remembered sayings of Jesus (same category as Didache 8:2, IV.6-c); the measure (VI.2-b, IV.8) and forgiveness/mercy
references.note: Two early fathers transmit clusters of dominical sayings introduced as Jesus's own words. 1 Clement 13:2 (c. 96): 'be merciful, that you may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven you; ... with the measure you measure, it will be measured to you' -- a chain blending the Beatitudes, the forgiveness sayings, and the measure-reciprocity (VI.2-b, IV.8). Polycarp, Phil. 2:3 (c. 110) gives a parallel chain ('judge not, that you be not judged; forgive, and you will be forgiven; be merciful...'). Same evidentiary category as the Didache's Lord's Prayer (IV.6-c): apostolic fathers citing remembered tradition. Their wording is synoptic-adjacent, so the independent value is low, but they confirm the early circulation of these sayings as Jesus's. Established as fathers' citations.
scholarship: Holmes, The Apostolic Fathers (texts and trans.)
Hagner, The Use of the OT and NT in Clement of Rome
